scenes.heading: Why a crescent, if the Moon is round?
scenes.text: Why does the Moon look like a crescent, when it is still a round world? Watch the light.

scenes.heading: One round Moon. One sunlit half.
scenes.text: The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight. Roughly half its surface is illuminated at once.

scenes.heading: Follow the view from Earth.
scenes.text: Now let the Moon move around Earth. From the ground, we see different fractions of that sunlit half. The shape we see changes; the Moon itself does not.

scenes.heading: New → first quarter → full
scenes.text: Near new Moon, the bright side faces away from us. At first quarter, half the visible disk is bright. First quarter means one quarter of the way through the phase cycle. Near full Moon, almost the entire disk is illuminated.

scenes.heading: A shadow is a different event.
scenes.text: These phases are not caused by Earth’s shadow. A lunar eclipse is different: Earth lies between the Sun and Moon, and its shadow reaches the Moon. That requires a special alignment.

scenes.heading: A cycle of about 29½ days
scenes.text: From one new Moon to the next takes about twenty nine and a half days. The bright portion grows and shrinks as our viewpoint changes.

scenes.heading: Same round world. A different view.
scenes.text: So that crescent is not a missing piece. It is a different view of a sunlit, round world. See differently.

editorial_intent: Replace the missing-piece intuition with a changing-view explanation; distinguish phases from eclipses.
